questions.topic: Two readings of a trust prosecution
questions.learningObjective: Describe the standard a 1911 decision announced for judging restraints of trade.
questions.stem: A note in the memo asks how a 1911 decision described the standard a court should apply to a combination of competitors.

answer.exemplar: The 1911 decision said a statute aimed at restraints of trade should not be read to condemn every agreement among competitors, but only those that unreasonably restrained competition, and that a court must judge each arrangement on its facts. That standard, commonly called the rule of reason, let ordinary cooperation survive while condemning the arrangements that actually suppressed rivals, and it explains why the same statute produced different results in different cases depending on what the combination actually did in the market.

questions.explanation: The rule of reason condemns only unreasonable restraints and lets a court weigh each arrangement, so one combination fell and another survived. A flat ban on all agreements ignores the standard.
questions.hint: Ask what the court must examine in each case.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: The referendum and the initiative side by side
questions.learningObjective: Explain what distinguishes a statutory referendum from a constitutional one.
questions.stem: The draft memorandum treats two kinds of referendum and explains the difference the voters would face.

answer.exemplar: The statutory referendum asks the electorate to accept or reject an ordinary law the legislature has passed, while the constitutional referendum puts a proposed change to the state's fundamental document before the voters, so that a later legislature cannot amend that document without the electorate's agreement. The practical difference lies in what follows the vote: a rejected statutory measure simply leaves the existing law in force, whereas a constitutional provision that the voters adopt becomes part of the state's structure and binds every later legislature.

questions.explanation: A statutory referendum reviews a law, while a constitutional referendum changes the basic document that binds later legislatures. The distinction lies in what the vote settles and what it constrains.
questions.hint: Which one changes the state's basic document?

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: Two readings of a delegated-power statute
questions.learningObjective: Explain the disagreement over the reach of a commerce power.
questions.stem: Under the planner's schedule, a note compares the reading that reached manufacturing with the reading that stopped at goods in transit.

answer.exemplar: The dispute turned on what counts as commerce. The narrow reading confines the clause to the movement of goods and people across state lines, so a factory making goods for shipment could be reached only by taxing its output rather than by regulating its working conditions, and a 1918 decision struck down a federal child-labour law on that ground. The broad reading treats commerce as a continuous web whose effects may be followed, so a factory's conditions become federal business whenever its products or raw materials move in interstate commerce.

questions.explanation: The dispute turned on what counts as commerce. The narrow reading confines the clause to movement across state lines, while the broad reading treats commerce as a web whose effects may be followed.
questions.hint: What counts as commerce: the goods or the chain?

questions.stem: Memo clause 9 provides that Congress may frame a general rule and let an agency fill in the details within limits.

answer.exemplar: The clause lets Congress set the aim and the outer boundaries of a rule while an agency works out the particulars, which is how detailed regulatory machinery was built without Congress spelling out every rule itself. The delegation is not unlimited: the statute must state the standard the agency applies and the limits it observes, and the agency must act within that frame and explain its choices, so the body doing the work has room to act but never room to reach beyond the purpose the legislature declared.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: The referendum and the initiative side by side
questions.learningObjective: Explain why reformers valued the initiative alongside the referendum.
questions.stem: A planner's note explains why reformers who already had the referendum still pressed for the initiative.

answer.exemplar: Reformers wanted the initiative because the referendum could only approve or reject what a legislature had already produced, and a legislature that answered to organised interests would rarely put a measure before the voters in the first place. The initiative closed that gap by letting citizens frame a proposal and gather signatures, so an issue the legislature ignored could still reach the ballot. Together the two tools gave voters a veto and an agenda, which is why campaigners treated them as complements rather than alternatives.

questions.explanation: The digest states that agents acting in the firm's own business are the firm, so the firm cannot distance itself from their conduct. The alternatives restrict responsibility or narrow the doctrine.
questions.hint: Who was held responsible for the agents' acts?

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: A health board on water treatment
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a health board tested water regularly rather than once.
questions.stem: The memo's public health appendix explains why a board kept sampling the reservoir after it had begun treating the water.

answer.exemplar: Sampling had to continue because a water supply is not a fixed thing. The reservoir receives runoff, sewage, and waste from the districts above it, so its condition changes with the season, with the weather, and with what households upstream did that week, and a supply that was clean when the works were built could be unsafe months later without anyone having touched the works themselves. The appendix makes the same point about the effect of treatment, which can be undone by a broken filter or a mistaken dose. Regular sampling was therefore the board's only way of knowing whether the protection it had paid for still held.

questions.explanation: Sampling had to continue because a reservoir's condition changes with runoff and upstream habits. A supply clean when the works were built could be unsafe months later.
questions.hint: A reservoir keeps changing after the works are built.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: The referendum and the initiative side by side
questions.learningObjective: Explain why some states used one tool and not the other.
questions.stem: Memo line 5 asks why reformers in one state won a referendum but lost an initiative campaign.

answer.exemplar: The referendum was the easier instrument to win because it rested on a law already passed, so the question could be put as a single yes or no about a measure whose text was known, and reform groups could fight over a specific proposal rather than over an idea. The initiative demanded more, because organisers had to draft a measure that had never been passed, persuade a majority of the electorate that the draft was the right answer, and then win a vote on it, which meant that a small group of well-organised enthusiasts could carry the first step and fail at the second. The memo notes that in the state in question the referendum petition had been signed by a broad coalition of reformers while the initiative campaign had rested on a single association's members.

questions.explanation: The referendum rested on a law already passed, so the vote could be one yes or no about a known text. The initiative demanded more, since organisers had to draft a measure and then win a vote on it.
questions.hint: Which campaign had to invent the text first?

options.text: A board could set the rents that landlords charged in any building it inspected

questions.hint: Regulating a nuisance is not the same as taking a house.
